title: Workshop Overview
content:
What You Will Build ReLoop connects device owners with verified repair and recycling partners while screening uploaded device photos with multimodal AI so listings stay clean, structured, and accurate. In this workshop you deploy the complete reloop2 stack using strictly serverless AWS services—zero EC2 instances, zero NAT Gateways, and pay-per-request scaling down to near zero when idle.
End-to-End Request Flows Static Web Delivery (/, all SPA routes): Browser connects over HTTPS -> Edge WAF (reloop2-web in us-east-1) -> CloudFront Distribution (PriceClass_200) -> CloudFront Function reloop2-spa-rewrite rewrites extensionless routes to /index.html while keeping dotted chat URLs (<partnerId>.<listingId>) intact -> private S3 web bucket via Origin Access Control (OAC). API & Authentication Calls (/api/*): Browser calls CloudFront /api/* -> CloudFront Function reloop2-api-prefix strips the /api prefix -> CloudFront forwards to HTTP API Gateway (reloop2-api in ap-southeast-1) injecting a shared secret header x-origin-verify -> API Gateway verifies JWT against Cognito (ANY /{proxy+}) or passes public routes -> Lambda (reloop2-api, Node.js 22 ARM64) validates x-origin-verify with timingSafeEqual and reads/writes DynamoDB. Direct Browser Image Upload & AI Analysis: Authenticated user requests a presigned upload from Lambda -> Browser uploads photo straight to private S3 bucket (reloop2-images-<suffix>) tagged state=pending -> On listing inspection, Lambda invokes Amazon Rekognition (DetectModerationLabels + DetectText OCR) -> screens extracted text with Amazon Bedrock Guardrail (ApplyGuardrailCommand) -> invokes Amazon Bedrock (global.moonshotai.kimi-k3) ConverseCommand to return structured device fields (title, category, brand, model, condition, defect description). Scheduled Maintenance & Alerts: Every 15 minutes, Amazon EventBridge rule reloop2-sweep invokes reloop2-api to expire 7-day open listings, issue 24-hour pickup reminders, and auto-complete 48-hour handoffs. CloudWatch Logs (7-day retention), a custom metric filter (UnhandledErrors), two CloudWatch metric alarms, SNS email alerts, and ReLoop2-Backend-Health provide live operational visibility. Security Highlights Layer Protection Mechanism Edge Network reloop2-web WAFv2 (CloudFront, us-east-1): 100 req/min rate limit on public endpoints, 1,000 req/min global IP ceiling, AWS IP Reputation List, Known Bad Inputs, Common Rule Set Browser Headers CloudFront Response Headers Policy (reloop2-security-headers): HSTS (max-age=31536000), X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, enforced frame-ancestors 'none' + CSP-Report-Only Origin Protection Both S3 buckets have Block Public Access ON (s3-web OAC-only, s3-images presigned-only); Lambda rejects any API request missing matching x-origin-verify header Identity Cognito User Pool protected by regional WAF reloop2-auth (ap-southeast-1, 300 auth calls / 5 min / IP), Pre-SignUp duplicate email guard, Deletion Protection ACTIVE, Auth Code PKCE Least Privilege IAM Separate Lambda execution roles (reloop2-post-confirmation-role and reloop2-api-lambda-role) scoped to explicit table ARNs, listings/* prefix, and required AI actions Workshop Cost Estimate Running the entire workshop from build through live E2E verification takes roughly 2–3 hours and is followed by a clean teardown in Module 5.13:
Service Usage During Workshop Estimated Cost DynamoDB On-demand reads/writes (<5 MB stored, PITR) ~$0.01 (Free Tier covers most) S3 Two private buckets, <20 MB assets & test photos <$0.01 Lambda & HTTP API Gateway ~100–300 invocations, 512 MB ARM64 $0.00 (Free Tier) Cognito Essentials tier, 1–5 test users $0.00 (Free Tier: 10,000 MAU) CloudFront <1 GB transfer, 2 CloudFront Functions $0.00 (Free Tier: 1 TB/mo) AWS WAFv2 2 Web ACLs x 7 rules prorated for ~1 day + 1K requests ~$0.25–$0.50 (or ~$12/mo if left running 30 days!) Bedrock & Rekognition ~5–15 test image moderations + Kimi K3 calls ~$0.05–$0.30 Total for Workshop Built, verified E2E, and deleted same day < $1.00 USD AWS WAFv2 Web ACLs charge $5/month per ACL + $1/month per rule continuously even with zero traffic. Complete Module 5.13 right after finishing Module 5.12 so your monthly bill remains minimal.
Repository & IaC Reference All resources built manually in Modules 5.2–5.11 are also captured as tested, modular Terraform configurations in the repository’s terraform/ directory (71/71 resources verified via import against the live stack with 0 to destroy). See Module 5.13 for usage details.

5 STEPS TO MANAGE AMAZON BEDROCK COSTS: BEYOND SIMPLY REDUCING TOKEN USAGE This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content When deploying Generative AI applications with Amazon Bedrock, costs depend on more than token consumption and model pricing. Identifying cost sources, monitoring resource usage, and implementing appropriate controls are also essential.
An AWS Machine Learning Blog article introduces a five-step cost management approach to help organizations monitor, control, and optimize Amazon Bedrock expenses throughout application operations.
Key Takeaways 1. Attribute Costs: Use AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0), IAM tags, and AWS Cost Explorer to analyze spending across users, teams, or applications. 2. Monitor Usage: Enable Model Invocation Logging to track model invocations and analyze token consumption using Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3. 3. Enforce Budget Controls: Combine AWS Budgets for alerts, IAM and automation for access restrictions, or an application gateway to control requests before model invocation. 4. Optimize Costs: Use Intelligent Prompt Routing, Prompt Caching, and appropriate token limits to reduce unnecessary resource consumption. 5. Review and Improve: Monitor model usage, failed requests, and Prompt Caching effectiveness to continuously refine cost-management policies. Practical Applications This approach is useful for Generative AI applications that need to manage costs across multiple users, teams, or workloads, especially as request volumes and token consumption increase.
Instead of reviewing billing reports only at the end of each month, organizations can combine usage data, budget alerts, and optimization techniques to proactively manage Amazon Bedrock costs.

title: Blog 2
content:
WHY CAN YOUR AWS BILL EXCEED A $10 BUDGET? This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content AWS Budgets helps users monitor cloud spending and receive alerts when costs reach predefined thresholds. However, setting a $10 budget does not mean AWS will automatically stop services once that amount is reached.
To reduce unexpected expenses, users need to understand the difference between budget notifications and actual cost-control mechanisms.
Key Takeaways AWS Budgets: Monitors actual or forecasted costs and sends notifications through email or Amazon SNS when configured thresholds are reached. Budgets are not hard spending limits: AWS services may continue running and generating charges even after the budget is exceeded. Budgets Actions: Allows users to apply IAM policies or perform actions on specified EC2/RDS instances when budget thresholds are reached. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection: Uses Machine Learning to identify unusual spending patterns and notify users of potential cost anomalies. AWS Cost Explorer: Helps analyze expenses by service, Region, or usage type to identify the sources of unexpected costs. Cost Data Latency: Billing information is not updated continuously in real time, so actual spending may exceed the configured threshold before an alert is delivered. Practical Applications For learning accounts and testing environments, AWS Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection, Cost Explorer, and Budgets Actions can be combined to monitor spending, detect unusual cost increases, and implement appropriate cost-control measures.
The key takeaway is that AWS Budgets does not guarantee that an account’s charges will never exceed the configured budget.

title: Proposal
content:
RELOOP An AI-assisted marketplace for used and damaged electronics, built on AWS serverless architecture 1. Executive Summary ReLoop is a web-based marketplace that enables users in Vietnam to sell used or damaged electronic devices (phones, laptops, monitors, and components) to nearby repair shops, electronics buyers, and recycling businesses. The project is developed by AWSS3nt1n4L, a five-member team participating in the AWS First Cloud Journey (FCAJ) program in Ho Chi Minh City, during a 12-week internship (September 14 – December 4, 2026).
Sellers upload photos, and Amazon Bedrock automatically suggests listing information. The listing is then distributed to all approved buyers whose branch service areas (1–15 km) cover the seller’s location. Transactions are finalized through buyer quotations or mutually agreed prices negotiated through chat.
As of November 8, 2026, the development environment had 14 accounts, 12 active listings from 7 sellers, and approximately 31,000 API requests during its first month. The serverless architecture supports scalability without requiring architectural redesign, with an approved Lambda concurrency quota of 1,000.
The primary AWS services include CloudFront, AWS WAF, API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito, Rekognition, Bedrock, EventBridge, CloudWatch, and SNS.
Guests can browse the Marketplace without an account. Authenticated users can chat and purchase items. Only Admin-approved partners can sell, while content moderation and invoice management are restricted to authorized Admin and Finance Admin roles.
Team Members Team Member Role Kung Cẩm Thành Team Lead Hoàng Quốc Việt Tech Lead Trần Hoàng Quốc Trung Backend Engineer Nguyễn Duy Quang Frontend Engineer Nguyễn Anh Kỳ Cybersecurity / Documentation 2. Problem Statement Current Challenges According to the Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (UNITAR/ITU), the world generated 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022, but only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled. According to the same report, Vietnam generated approximately 516,000 tonnes of electronic waste (approximately 5.3 kg per capita) in 2022.
Owners of used or damaged electronic devices often do not know who is willing to purchase their devices or how much those devices are worth. Currently, they rely on general classified websites or social media groups, manually describe their devices, contact individual repair shops, and frequently receive no response.
General marketplaces such as Chợ Tốt and Facebook Marketplace serve a wide range of product categories and therefore lack:
Listing matching based on repair shops’ service areas covering the seller’s location. Estimated prices calculated according to individual buyers’ pricing rules. Reputation records reflecting whether buyers honor their quotations. Small repair shops face similar challenges from the buyer’s perspective, as they lack an affordable channel for receiving relevant electronic devices from nearby sellers.
Solution ReLoop operates entirely on managed AWS services without requiring the team to maintain dedicated servers.
Ingestion: browsers upload up to 6 images per listing (JPEG/PNG/WebP, up to 5 MB per image) directly to Amazon S3 using presigned POST URLs. Amazon Rekognition performs image content moderation and text detection. Detected text is evaluated through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to identify suspicious content and route it for Admin review.
Processing: a single AWS Lambda function (Node.js 22, arm64) serves 111 API routes behind Amazon API Gateway. The function also invokes itself asynchronously for time-consuming tasks:
AI-powered image analysis using Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock, taking approximately 35 seconds per analysis. Matching listings with buyer branches using geohash and Haversine calculations. Amazon EventBridge invokes the same function every 15 minutes to process expired listings, automatically complete transactions after 48 hours, send reminders, and generate monthly invoices.
Storage: a single Amazon DynamoDB table (PK/SK + 1 GSI) stores all entity types, including users, partners, branches, pricing rules, listings, quotations, transactions, chats, reviews, invoices, and Admin audit records. Write operations are conditional, and financial API operations require an Idempotency-Key. S3 Lifecycle rules delete unused images after 1 day and all images after 90 days.
Web Interface: a React single-page application served from a private S3 bucket through Amazon CloudFront. It includes a public Marketplace, a two-tier partner portal, and an Admin portal.
Security: Amazon Cognito manages user authentication and authorization. API Gateway validates JWTs on private routes. AWS WAF helps protect the web application and authentication process. The platform applies Content-Security-Policy (CSP) and the principle of Least Privilege through AWS IAM.
Compared with general classified platforms, ReLoop provides AI-assisted listing creation, service-area matching, rule-based price estimation, two-step transaction completion (seller confirms the final price and buyer accepts it), and two-way reviews.
ReLoop does not process payments directly. Both parties handle payments independently during device handover.
Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI) Reduced manual input: AI suggests the title, category, brand, model, and condition of electronic devices from up to 3 images. Sellers only need to confirm or modify the suggestions. Creating a listing takes approximately 5 minutes manually and less than 1 minute with AI assistance, based on the team’s estimates. Fewer unanswered listings: each new listing is automatically matched with buyer branches within their service areas, with branches within 5 km prioritized. Reliability: state machines, conditional writes, and idempotent background jobs maintain consistency across listings, quotations, and transactions. The project includes 182 automated tests and an end-to-end smoke test running on AWS. Learning value: the team gains practical experience in DynamoDB single-table design, event-driven Lambda processing, structured JSON responses from Bedrock, Infrastructure as Code using Terraform, AWS WAF configuration, and security testing. Cost efficiency: approximately USD 18.70/month (USD 224.40/year) at the current scale (Section 6). AWS WAF accounts for USD 17.00 of this amount. Without WAF, the estimated infrastructure cost would be approximately USD 1.70/month. Until February 28, 2027, costs are covered by the remaining AWS account credits (USD 197.14 as of November 8, 2026). Break-even point: revenue is generated through a VND 10,000 fee paid by the seller for each completed transaction. Assuming an approximate exchange rate of USD 1 ≈ VND 26,000 in November 2026, USD 18.70 is equivalent to approximately VND 486,200. Therefore, the platform reaches infrastructure cost break-even at 49 completed transactions per month, or 5 transactions per month under a cost scenario excluding WAF. 3. Solution Architecture ReLoop uses a serverless architecture with backend resources deployed in the ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) region:
AWS WAF and Amazon CloudFront protect and distribute web application content. Static files are served from a private S3 bucket, while API requests are forwarded to Amazon API Gateway. A single Lambda function contains the application’s business logic. It interacts with DynamoDB, S3, Rekognition, and Bedrock through lightweight adapters, allowing the same codebase to run locally using Node.js and in-memory storage. Amazon Cognito manages user registration, sign-in, and authentication. Application logs and business metrics are collected by CloudWatch. SNS sends email notifications to administrators when alarms are triggered. All infrastructure is defined using Terraform, with its state stored in a versioned S3 bucket. Original architecture diagram: reloop-architecture.drawio (generated using diagram/make_architecture.py).
AWS Services Used Amazon CloudFront: delivers the web application and forwards /api/* requests to API Gateway. Implements security headers such as CSP, HSTS, and X-Frame-Options. AWS WAF: uses two Web ACLs to protect the web application and authentication system, combining AWS Managed Rules with rate-limiting mechanisms. Amazon S3: uses three buckets for the web application build (private, with OAC), device images (presigned POST/GET and tag-based lifecycle management), and Terraform state (with versioning). Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API): validates JWTs on private routes and applies throttling to control API traffic. AWS Lambda: runs Node.js 22 on arm64 (Graviton) with 512 MB of memory. Handles API requests, asynchronous AI and matching workers, scheduled jobs, and Cognito pre-sign-up triggers. The average execution duration is 144 ms, with a concurrency quota of 1,000. Amazon DynamoDB: uses a single on-demand table with PK/SK and GSI1, with PITR and TTL enabled (notifications automatically expire after 90 days). Currently contains approximately 5,600 records (2.4 MB). Amazon Cognito: provides an email-verified user pool and manages user authorization groups. Currently supports 14 users. Amazon Rekognition: performs image content moderation and text detection. Amazon Bedrock: uses Kimi K3 through the Converse API with tool choice to generate structured JSON responses. Guardrails support content filtering and AI safety. Amazon EventBridge: uses one scheduled rule that runs every 15 minutes to invoke background processing jobs. Amazon CloudWatch: provides application logs, custom business metrics, one dashboard, and 10 alarms for system monitoring. Amazon SNS: delivers email alerts to administrators. AWS IAM: manages resource access permissions according to the principle of Least Privilege. AWS Security Agent: performs automated security testing on the development environment (3.63 task-hours on November 8, 2026; remediation updates deployed on November 10, 2026). Component Design Edge / Client: a React 18 + TypeScript single-page application built with Vite, using Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for location selection. Guests can browse the Marketplace. After authentication, users can access the partner portal (Tier 1: individual sellers, up to 3 active listings; Tier 2: businesses with branches, pricing rules, and quotations, up to 10 active listings) or the Admin portal.
Ingestion:
The system generates a presigned POST URL, allowing browsers to upload images directly to Amazon S3. Amazon Rekognition performs image content moderation. When a listing is created, the system updates the image status to support appropriate storage lifecycle management. Processing: the HTTP router handles authentication, idempotency, and input validation. State machines for Listing, Quote, and Transaction enforce valid state transitions. AI processing and listing matching run asynchronously. The background job runner organizes tasks by time intervals to identify scheduled work without scanning the entire table.
Storage: data access patterns are defined in backend/src/store/keys.ts. Marketplace listings are partitioned by month, with cursor-based pagination and cursor format validation. Monetary values are stored as integer VND amounts.
Web Interface: a public Marketplace, listing-specific chat (updated every 5 seconds) with price negotiation, transaction management (handover scheduling, price adjustments, confirmation, and disputes), and reviews.
User Management: Cognito registration requires email verification. The system validates registered accounts. Administrators approve partner applications, while Finance Admins generate and confirm monthly invoices. Sellers with invoices overdue by more than 3 days cannot create new listings; accounts with invoices overdue by more than 7 days are suspended.
Monitoring: structured JSON logs, metric filters for business events, CloudWatch dashboards, SNS email notifications, and WAF log management with sensitive information protection.

The adapter-based design (Table, ImageStore, Analyzer, AuthProvider) allows services to be replaced or extended, such as SES-based email delivery, WebSocket chat, or banking payment APIs, without modifying the core business logic. The same Terraform configuration and deployment scripts can be used to establish a production environment or expand the platform to another city. Geohash-based listing matching can operate across different geographical locations. Repair shops and recycling businesses gain an additional reliable channel for receiving used electronic devices from nearby sellers. This contributes to device reuse and formal recycling rather than allowing unused electronics to accumulate in households.

title: DynamoDB Single-Table Data Layer
content:
ReLoop uses an Amazon DynamoDB single-table schema (reloop2-core-table) in ap-southeast-1 with On-Demand capacity, one Global Secondary Index (GSI1) for role/status queries, 35-day Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR), and Time to Live (TTL) for automatic cleanup of temporary records and timers.
Single-Table Key Design Overview Attribute Type Role PK String (S) Partition Key — entity prefix (USER#<id>, LISTING#<id>, TIMER#<isoTime>, SESSION#<id>) SK String (S) Sort Key — record subtype (PROFILE, META, QUOTE#<id>, LISTING_EXPIRE#<id>) GSI1PK String (S) Secondary partition key (ROLE#Owner, STATUS#OPEN, PARTNER#<id>) GSI1SK String (S) Secondary sort key (USER#<id>, <createdAt>) ttl Number (N) Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) monitored by DynamoDB TTL Step 1 — Create reloop2-core-table Switch back to Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1, open DynamoDB -> Tables, and click Create table. Under Table details: Table name: reloop2-core-table Partition key: PK (String) Sort key: SK (String) Select Customize settings, set Capacity mode to On-demand, then scroll to Secondary indexes -> click Create global index: Partition key: GSI1PK (String) Sort key: GSI1SK (String) Index name: GSI1 Attribute projections: All Review the complete configuration summary (On-demand throughput + Standard table class + GSI1). Confirm Secondary indexes shows GSI1 queued with ALL projection. Under Tags, add standard workshop tags: Owner = team Project = reloop2 Purpose = workshop Then click Create table. Wait ~15 seconds while the table status transitions from Creating to Active. Step 2 — Enable Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) & TTL Open reloop2-core-table -> Backups tab -> under Point-in-time recovery (PITR) click Edit. Check Turn on point-in-time recovery and set Recovery window (days) to 35, then click Save changes. Scroll to Additional settings -> Time to Live (TTL) -> click Turn on -> enter TTL attribute name: ttl -> Turn on TTL. Step 3 — Verify Table & Index Status Open the Overview tab and Indexes tab of reloop2-core-table to confirm: Status is Active Billing mode is On-demand GSI1 is Active with PK/SK + GSI1PK/GSI1SK (ALL)

title: Blog 3
content:
WHY DOES AN API STILL NEED THROTTLING WHEN AWS WAF IS ALREADY ENABLED? This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content When an API receives a large volume of requests, AWS WAF alone may not be sufficient to control all traffic reaching the backend. AWS WAF and API Gateway Throttling serve different purposes: one filters suspicious traffic early, while the other controls request rates before backend execution.
The example architecture follows Client → Amazon CloudFront (AWS WAF) → Amazon API Gateway → AWS Lambda, with Amazon CloudWatch providing monitoring across the protection layers.
Key Takeaways AWS WAF Rate-based Rules: Monitor request frequency by IP address or other configured aggregation criteria to limit unusual traffic before it reaches API Gateway. Scope-down Statements: Allow rate-based rules to target specific endpoints, such as /api/search, instead of the entire website. API Gateway Throttling: Uses Rate Limits and Burst Limits to control request traffic and reduce pressure on AWS Lambda. HTTP 403 and 429: AWS WAF returns HTTP 403 by default for blocked requests, while API Gateway may return HTTP 429 when throttling limits are exceeded. Direct API Access: If the default execute-api endpoint remains accessible, clients may bypass the WAF protection associated with CloudFront. CloudWatch Monitoring: Combines WAF logs, API Gateway metrics/access logs, and Lambda metrics to identify where requests are blocked or processed. Practical Applications For public APIs, combining AWS WAF with API Gateway Throttling helps limit unusual traffic, manage backend workloads, and reduce the risk of disrupting legitimate users.
A recommended approach is to test WAF Rate-based Rules using the Count action before switching to Block. Direct access to API Gateway should also be reviewed, while logs and metrics are monitored to verify the effectiveness of each protection layer.

title: Cognito Authentication & Profile Sync
content:
In this module you configure Amazon Cognito (reloop2-user-pool), define RBAC user groups (Admins, FinanceAdmins, Partners, Owners), enable Managed Login v2 on domain reloop2-auth, and create the Python 3.12 Post-Confirmation Lambda (reloop2-post-confirmation) that writes every newly verified user straight into reloop2-core-table.
Part A — Create User Pool & Configure Authentication Open Amazon Cognito -> User pools in ap-southeast-1 and click Create user pool. In the Set up your application wizard: Choose Single-page application (SPA) Name your application client reloop2-web-client Select Email as the sign-in identifier and email, name as required sign-up attributes, then click Create user directory. Once Cognito creates the pool, review the generated User Pool ID and click Go to overview. On Overview, click Rename, enter reloop2-user-pool, and save. Under Authentication -> Authentication methods: verify Password (PASSWORD) is enabled and MFA is No MFA (Essentials tier default for smoother workshop onboarding; enable TOTP/SMS for production). Under Authentication -> Sign-in: confirm Email sign-in (alias_attributes = ["email"]) and case-insensitive usernames. Under Sign-up -> Attribute verification and user account confirmation: ensure self-service sign-up is on, email verification is active, and Account recovery uses Email only (verified_email, priority 1). Add workshop tags (Owner = team, Project = reloop2, Purpose = workshop) and confirm Deletion protection is Active (we will deactivate it explicitly in Module 5.13). Part B — Create User Groups (RBAC) Go to User management -> Groups and create all 4 groups: Group Name Precedence Description Admins 1 System operators and verifiers FinanceAdmins 1 Finance reconcilers (bank / payout approvals) Partners 2 Verified recycling and repair shops Owners 3 Device sellers Part C — Configure App Client (reloop2-web-client) & Managed Login Domain Open Applications -> App clients -> reloop2-web-client: check Authentication flows allow ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH and ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH, access/ID token validity is 60 minutes, refresh token validity is 5 days, and Prevent user existence errors is enabled. Click the Login pages tab -> Edit Managed Login pages configuration: Temporarily set Allowed callback URLs to http://localhost:5173/auth/callback Temporarily set Allowed sign-out URLs to http://localhost:5173/ (we will append the CloudFront HTTPS URL in Module 5.8 once CloudFront is created!) OAuth 2.0 grant types: Authorization code grant (code) OpenID Connect scopes: openid, email, phone Go to Branding -> Domain. Cognito creates an auto-generated domain initially; create/replace with custom Cognito prefix reloop2-auth using Managed login version 2 (https://reloop2-auth.auth.ap-southeast-1.amazoncognito.com). title: Blog 4
content:
AMAZON BEDROCK: CONTROLLING REQUESTS AND TOKEN USAGE BEFORE COSTS INCREASE This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content When deploying Generative AI applications with Amazon Bedrock, limiting the number of API requests alone is not sufficient for effective cost management. Even valid requests can consume large numbers of tokens due to long prompts or extensive outputs, especially in multi-tenant applications.
To reduce unexpected expenses, a layered architecture can combine Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, API Gateway, AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock, supported by monitoring and usage analytics services.
Key Takeaways AWS WAF and Amazon CloudFront: Filter unusual traffic at the edge using Rate-based Rules, reducing unnecessary requests before they reach the application. Amazon API Gateway: Provides authentication, authorization, and throttling through Rate Limits and Burst Limits to control incoming traffic. AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB: Implement a Quota Controller to enforce per-tenant request or token limits before invoking Bedrock. Atomic and Conditional Updates: Help maintain accurate quota records when multiple requests are processed concurrently. Token Usage Tracking: Estimates token consumption before inference and reconciles it with actual usage after Bedrock returns a response. Amazon CloudWatch and SNS: Monitor model invocations, input/output tokens, and send notifications when usage exceeds configured thresholds. Amazon S3 and Athena: Store and analyze usage data by tenant, model, or time period to support more detailed cost management. Practical Applications This architecture is useful for AI applications serving multiple users or tenants, where individual usage limits are needed to reduce unexpected costs caused by repeated requests or excessive token consumption.
For smaller applications, Lambda, DynamoDB, and CloudWatch can provide a practical starting point. S3 and Athena can be introduced later when more advanced usage analysis is required.
Application-level quotas must also account for concurrent requests, retries, and differences between estimated and actual token usage. These controls help reduce unexpected consumption but do not guarantee an absolute spending limit.

title: S3 Private Images, CORS & Lifecycle
content:
Uploaded device photos go directly from the user’s browser to a private Amazon S3 bucket (reloop2-images-<suffix>, e.g. reloop2-images-7k3q) via short-lived presigned URLs issued by Lambda. Block All Public Access stays enabled so photos cannot be listed or hotlinked outside controlled presigned URLs, while CORS allows browser uploads and S3 Lifecycle rules automatically purge abandoned pending uploads and incomplete multipart uploads.
Step 1 — Create Private Bucket reloop2-images-<suffix> Open Amazon S3 -> Buckets in ap-southeast-1 and click Create bucket. Configure General configuration: AWS Region: ap-southeast-1 Bucket type: General purpose Bucket name: reloop2-images-7k3q (replace 7k3q with your own globally unique 4-character suffix) Leave Block all public access checked (ON) — never expose raw user photos via public bucket policies. Add workshop tags (Owner=team, Project=reloop2, Purpose=workshop), keep SSE-S3 (AES256) with Bucket Key Enabled, and click Create bucket. Step 2 — Configure CORS for Direct Browser Uploads Open reloop2-images-7k3q -> Permissions -> scroll to Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) -> click Edit and paste (we start with http://localhost:5173, then append our CloudFront origin in Module 5.8): [ { "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "POST", "GET"], "AllowedOrigins": ["http://localhost:5173"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"] } ] Step 3 — Add 3 Cost-Control Lifecycle Rules Open Management -> Lifecycle rules -> click Create lifecycle rule for each rule below: Rule Name Scope / Filter Action reloop2-listing-images-unattached Prefix listings/ AND object tag state = pending Expire current versions after 1 day reloop2-listing-images-retention Prefix listings/ (all attached photos) Expire current versions after 90 days reloop2-abort-incomplete-uploads Prefix listings/ Abort incomplete multipart uploads after 1 day Confirm all 3 lifecycle rules show status Enabled under Management -> Lifecycle rules.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Internship Reflections & Constructive Feedback During my participation in the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) internship program, I have had the opportunity to explore cloud computing, learn about Amazon Web Services (AWS), attend technology events, and experience the process of working on a project with my team members.
As an Information Security student at FPT University, participating in the First Cloud AI Journey program has provided me with an opportunity to broaden my knowledge beyond my academic specialization. Through exploring AWS services and collaborating with my team on a practical project, I have gained additional perspectives on how technology systems and applications are developed, deployed, and operated in real-world environments.
Beyond technical knowledge, the program has also provided valuable experiences in workplace environments, independent learning, teamwork, and technical documentation.
Evaluation of the Program 1. Learning and Working Environment I appreciate the flexible learning environment provided by the FCAJ program, where students can independently research documentation, practice at home, register for office working sessions, and participate in community activities.
Working at the office provides opportunities to interact with students from different universities, communicate directly with team members, and become familiar with a practical working environment.
Participating in events such as Buildrathon Kickoff, AWS Cloud & AI Day, FCAJ Meetup, and Cloud Mastery has also allowed me to explore various technology topics, learn from experienced professionals, and broaden my perspective on the information technology industry.
2. Learning Resources and Mentorship The learning materials and workshops provided by the AWS Study Group are valuable resources that help me gradually become familiar with AWS services and independently explore new topics.
The program emphasizes independent learning and research. This presents both an opportunity and a challenge for students with limited experience in cloud computing.
Guidance from mentors, combined with discussions among team members, has helped me identify relevant learning topics and gradually adapt to the program’s requirements.
3. Technical Knowledge and Practical Relevance Although cloud computing is not the primary focus of my current academic specialization, the knowledge gained from the program remains a valuable supplement to my studies.
Exploring services such as AWS IAM, Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS WAF has helped me better understand resource management, access control, system protection, and monitoring in cloud environments.
Additionally, researching AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer, and the costs associated with AI services has helped me recognize that developing a practical system requires consideration not only of technical requirements but also of operational costs and resource efficiency.
These additional perspectives and areas of knowledge may prove useful in my future studies and professional activities.
4. Teamwork Experience in the ReLoop Project Participating in the ReLoop project with the AWSS3nt1n4L team has been one of the notable experiences of my internship.
Each team member has different knowledge, strengths, and responsibilities. In my cybersecurity and documentation role, I focus on understanding the system, researching security-related topics, participating in website testing, documenting identified issues, and contributing to project documentation.
Through collaborative work, I have gained a better understanding of how different roles contribute to a technology project, including frontend development, business logic implementation, AI integration, testing, and documentation.
This experience has also helped me recognize that team members can contribute to shared outcomes through different responsibilities without necessarily participating directly in every stage of system development.
5. Personal Skills Development In addition to acquiring knowledge about AWS, the program has provided opportunities to improve my independent learning, information research, knowledge organization, and technical communication skills.
Writing four technical blog posts, maintaining weekly worklogs, documenting technology events, and preparing the Proposal and Workshop have helped me improve my ability to organize and present technical information.
Building a bilingual internship report website using Hugo, managing source files through GitHub, and deploying the website through GitHub Pages have also introduced me to online documentation management and publishing workflows.
These skills are applicable across different areas of information technology, rather than being limited to cloud computing.
Retrospective Questions What are you most proud of during your internship? One of the most meaningful aspects of my internship is the opportunity to explore a technology field outside the primary focus of my academic specialization, gradually become familiar with AWS services, and participate in a practical team project.
Although I am not directly responsible for the entire development or deployment process of ReLoop, I have had opportunities to contribute through research, testing, issue documentation, and technical documentation.
Completing four technical blog posts and building my personal internship report website are also meaningful achievements. These deliverables reflect my efforts to research, consolidate knowledge, and complete the assigned internship activities.
What could the program organizers improve for future cohorts? Clarify internship report requirements
I would appreciate more detailed guidance regarding the expected content and scope of each report section, particularly the Proposal and Workshop for team-based projects. Clearly distinguishing shared project outcomes from individual contributions would help students prepare their documentation more effectively.
Provide learning paths for different academic backgrounds
Students participating in the program may come from various academic disciplines, including Software Engineering, Information Security, Artificial Intelligence, and related fields. In addition to the foundational AWS learning path, the program could recommend optional learning directions or topics suited to different academic backgrounds.
Strengthen AWS cost management guidance
For students who are new to cloud computing, managing costs and using AWS Credits effectively are important considerations. The program could provide more practical examples of service costs, resource monitoring, and precautions when practicing with AWS services.
Introduce additional progress reviews and discussion sessions
Additional short discussions between mentors and project teams at different development stages would provide opportunities for students to present their progress, clarify difficulties, and receive feedback before completing their products and final reports.
Encourage interaction between project teams
Knowledge-sharing sessions covering project ideas, system architectures, implementation experiences, and encountered challenges would allow students to learn from other teams participating in the program.
Would you recommend the program to your friends and junior students? Yes. I would recommend the First Cloud AI Journey program to students interested in exploring cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and AWS services.
For students from other academic disciplines, the program can also provide an opportunity to broaden their knowledge, gain teamwork experience, and explore technologies used in practical environments.
However, I believe that each student should consider their learning objectives, career direction, and the program’s relevance to their academic specialization to make the most of their internship experience.
Future Development Direction After the internship, I intend to continue developing my knowledge and skills in my Information Security specialization.
The cloud computing and AWS knowledge acquired throughout the program will serve as a supplementary foundation, providing additional perspectives on the deployment and operation of information technology systems.
I also aim to continue improving my independent learning, practical skills, technical English, teamwork, and technical documentation abilities to support my future studies and professional activities.
Acknowledgments I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the First Cloud AI Journey organizers, mentors, and AWS Study Group community for providing opportunities to acquire new knowledge, participate in technology activities, and experience a practical internship environment.
I would also like to thank the members of the AWSS3nt1n4L team for their communication, support, and collaboration throughout the ReLoop project.
The knowledge, experiences, and lessons gained during this internship will remain valuable to my continued learning and personal development.
I wish the First Cloud AI Journey program continued growth and success in providing meaningful learning opportunities and practical experiences for future generations of students.

title: AI Content Safety with Bedrock Guardrails
content:
ReLoop runs a multi-stage screening pipeline whenever a user analyzes device photos:
Amazon Rekognition (DetectModerationLabels + DetectText) runs on the S3 photo in ap-southeast-1. Any text detected by OCR (for example printed labels, serial stickers, or offensive text injected into a photo) is screened through Amazon Bedrock Guardrail (reloop2-ai-guardrail) via ApplyGuardrailCommand. If screening passes, Amazon Bedrock (global.moonshotai.kimi-k3) executes ConverseCommand to inspect the device photos and return structured JSON attributes. Important Runtime Note on Kimi K3: In Bedrock Runtime (index.js), when AI_MODEL_ID contains kimi, ReLoop calls ConverseCommand without inline guardrailConfig (and uses maxTokens: 2048 without a custom temperature), because Kimi K3’s cross-region inference profile does not accept inline guardrailConfig. Instead, safety enforcement still invokes your published Guardrail directly via ApplyGuardrailCommand (bedrock:ApplyGuardrail permission in Module 5.6)!
Step 1 — Create Guardrail reloop2-ai-guardrail Open Amazon Bedrock -> Guardrails (verify Cross-region inference is available in ap-southeast-1 or configure guardrail-profile/apac.guardrail.v1:0) and click Create guardrail. Configure Guardrail details: Name: reloop2-ai-guardrail Description: ReLoop 2: filter unsafe text and images during AI device analysis Messaging for blocked prompts: Ảnh không phù hợp. Messaging for blocked responses: Kết quả không phù hợp. Enable Cross-region inference (apac.guardrail.v1:0) and add standard workshop tags (Owner=team, Project=reloop2, Purpose=workshop). Step 2 — Configure Content Filters (Standard Tier, HIGH) Under Content filters: select Standard tier and configure all 6 categories at HIGH threshold with BLOCK action: Category Input Modalities Input Strength Output Modalities Output Strength Hate TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Insults TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Sexual TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Violence TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Misconduct TEXT HIGH TEXT HIGH Prompt Attack TEXT HIGH (N/A) NONE Review all details and filters, then click Create guardrail. Step 3 — Test in Bedrock Guardrail Playground & Publish Version 1 Inside reloop2-ai-guardrail, test unsafe / prompt-injection text (Ignore previous instructions...) and confirm the Guardrail blocks it with "Ảnh không phù hợp." and displays a GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED trace. Next test a benign electronic device prompt (Dell Latitude laptop with cracked screen corner, battery missing) and verify it passes cleanly without intervention. Click Versions -> Create version, enter description v1 cho reloop2-api (ReLoop 2 workshop), and publish Version 1 (immutable snapshot for production/workshop stability). Step 4 — Wire Guardrail ID & Version to reloop2-api Lambda Open AWS Lambda -> reloop2-api -> Configuration -> Environment variables -> Edit, add: AI_GUARDRAIL_ID = <your guardrail ID> (e.g. a1b2c3d4e5f6) AI_GUARDRAIL_VERSION = 1 Save and verify.

title: Frontend SPA, CloudFront & Origin Access
content:
In this module you host the React/Vite Single-Page Application (SPA) inside a completely private S3 bucket (reloop2-web-7k3q), expose both the frontend and /api/* under a single Amazon CloudFront HTTPS origin using Origin Access Control (OAC), attach two lightweight CloudFront Functions, enforce strict Security Headers, lock direct API Gateway bypasses with x-origin-verify, and complete the CORS + Cognito URL backfill.
Part A — Create Private Web Bucket (reloop2-web-<suffix>) & Upload Bundle Open S3 -> Create bucket in ap-southeast-1, name it reloop2-web-7k3q (same unique suffix as reloop2-images), keep Block all public access ON, add tags, and keep SSE-S3 + Bucket Key. Build your React frontend (npm run build) with VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID, VITE_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID, VITE_COGNITO_DOMAIN, and VITE_API_BASE=/api, then upload index.html and the assets/ folder into reloop2-web-7k3q. Part B — Create Two CloudFront Functions (cloudfront-js-2.0) Go to CloudFront -> Functions -> Create function (runtime cloudfront-js-2.0): Function 1: reloop2-spa-rewrite — rewrites client-side React routes to /index.html ONLY when the URI does NOT end with a real static file extension (crucial for ReLoop chat routes formatted like /chat/<partnerId>.<listingId>, which contain a . but are not static files!): function handler(event) { var req = event.request; // Only real asset extensions pass; chat route "<partnerId>.<listingId>" also contains a dot if (!/\.(js|mjs|css|map|html|png|jpe?g|gif|svg|ico|webp|avif|txt|json|xml|webmanifest|woff2?|ttf)$/i.test(req.uri)) req.uri = '/index.html'; return req; } Function 2: reloop2-api-prefix — strips the leading /api prefix before CloudFront forwards requests to HTTP API Gateway (<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com): function handler(event) { var req = event.request; req.uri = req.uri.replace(/^\/api(?=\/)/, ''); return req; } Part C — Create Security Response Headers Policy & OAC Go to CloudFront -> Policies -> Response headers -> Create response headers policy: Name: reloop2-security-headers Security headers (all Override checked): Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff X-Frame-Options: DENY Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self' Custom header: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only (Override ON) allowing 'self', Google Fonts, S3 images bucket reloop2-images-7k3q.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com, Cognito IDP & Hosted UI domain, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim tiles. Go to CloudFront -> Security -> Origin access -> Create control setting: Name: reloop2-web Signing behavior: Sign requests (recommended) (always), SigV4, Origin type S3. Part D — Create Distribution, Dual Origins & Dual Behaviors Open CloudFront -> Distributions -> Create distribution: Use Pay as you go (PriceClass_200) Point first origin to reloop2-web-7k3q.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com using OAC reloop2-web, default root object index.html, HTTP/2 + HTTP/3 (http2and3), IPv6 disabled (is_ipv6_enabled = false) Choose Do not enable security protections during the initial wizard (we attach a customized rate-limited WAF in Module 5.9!) Under General -> Settings -> Edit, verify Default root object is index.html and Supported HTTP versions is HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Open the Origins tab and add the second origin (api): Origin domain: <api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com (strip https://) Protocol: HTTPS only, TLSv1.2 minimum, Read timeout 30s, Keep-alive 5s Add custom header: x-origin-verify = <exact ORIGIN_VERIFY_SECRET value from Lambda> Open the Behaviors tab: Edit Default (*) behavior: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, CachingOptimized, Response headers policy reloop2-security-headers, and Viewer request Function association -> reloop2-spa-rewrite. Create behavior for /api/* -> Target origin api: HTTPS only, Allowed methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE, Cache policy CachingDisabled, Origin request policy AllViewerExceptHostHeader, Response headers policy reloop2-security-headers, and Viewer request Function association -> reloop2-api-prefix. Copy CloudFront’s generated S3 bucket policy and paste it into reloop2-web-7k3q -> Permissions -> Bucket policy (CloudFrontRead s3:GetObject + CloudFrontList s3:ListBucket scoped strictly with StringEquals on AWS:SourceArn of your CloudFront Distribution ARN). Part E — Critical Backfill: Update CORS & Cognito URLs with CloudFront Domain Now that your CloudFront domain (https://<dist-domain>.cloudfront.net) exists, immediately update all three downstream services so authentication and uploads work smoothly:
Cognito (reloop2-user-pool -> App client reloop2-web-client -> Login pages): append https://<dist-domain>.cloudfront.net/auth/callback and https://<dist-domain>.cloudfront.net/. S3 (reloop2-images-7k3q -> Permissions -> CORS): append "https://<dist-domain>.cloudfront.net" to AllowedOrigins. API Gateway (reloop2-api -> Develop -> CORS): append https://<dist-domain>.cloudfront.net to Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Run an Invalidation (/*) on your CloudFront distribution so edge caches pick up the fresh bundle and headers right away.

title: Edge & Cognito Security with AWS WAFv2
content:
In this module you add two layered AWS WAFv2 Web ACLs:
Edge Web ACL (reloop2-web) in Global (us-east-1) attached directly to your CloudFront distribution — enforces endpoint-specific rate limiting, global IP ceilings, AWS Managed Rules (AmazonIpReputationList, KnownBadInputsRuleSet, CommonRuleSet tuned to avoid false blocks on photo payloads). Regional Web ACL (reloop2-auth) in Singapore (ap-southeast-1) attached directly to your Cognito User Pool — throttles credential stuffing and sign-up spam against 7 specific Cognito actions (300 requests / 5 minutes / IP). Part A — Create Edge Web ACL (reloop2-web in us-east-1) Switch your Console region to Global (CloudFront) or US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1 before creating reloop2-web. CloudFront WAF Web ACLs cannot be created from ap-southeast-1.
Open AWS WAF -> Web ACLs, select Global (CloudFront), and click Create web ACL. Under Step 1 — Describe web ACL and associate it to AWS resources: Name: reloop2-web Description: ReLoop 2: IP rate limits, bad IPs, common attack patterns - CloudFront Associated AWS resources: Click Add AWS resources and attach your CloudFront distribution. Add all 5 rules in priority order 0..4: Priority 0 — rate-limit-public-api: Rate-based rule (100 requests / 60-second window per IP) scoped down (OR) to URI path prefix (LOWERCASE, STARTS_WITH) matching /api/auth/, /api/feed/public, or /api/fees. Action: Block returning HTTP 429 JSON custom response (rate_limited, header retry-after: 60): {"code":"RATE_LIMITED","message":"Too many requests - wait about 1 minute and try again"} Priority 1 — rate-limit-per-ip: Rate-based rule (1000 requests / 60-second window per IP across all paths) returning the same HTTP 429 custom JSON response. Priority 2, 3, 4 — AWS Managed Free Rule Groups: AWS-AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList AWS-AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet AWS-AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet — edit sub-rules and set SizeRestrictions_BODY and GenericRFI_BODY overrides to Count so rich JSON listing payloads or external map URLs do not trigger false 403 blocks! Verify the 5 rules, confirm Priority ordering (0 to 4), keep CloudWatch metrics + sampled requests enabled, review, and click Create web ACL. Part B — Create Regional Auth Web ACL (reloop2-auth in ap-southeast-1) Switch back to Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 in AWS WAF -> Create web ACL. Name it reloop2-auth, Description ReLoop 2: brute-force and sign-up spam protection - Cognito, and under Associated AWS resources select Amazon Cognito user pools -> reloop2-user-pool. Add 2 rules: Priority 0 — rate-limit-auth: Rate-based rule (300 requests / 300-second window per IP) scoped down when HTTP header x-amzn-cognito-operation-name (EXACTLY) matches any of: InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, SignUp, ConfirmSignUp, ResendConfirmationCode, ForgotPassword, ConfirmForgotPassword. Action: Block. Priority 1 — AWS-AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList. Review, create reloop2-auth, and confirm reloop2-user-pool shows under Associated AWS resources.

title: Observability: Logs, Alarms, SNS & Dashboard
content:
In this module you establish cost-controlled logging (7-day retention), extract a structured metric from Lambda JSON error logs, wire SNS email alerts, configure two actionable CloudWatch Metric Alarms, and assemble the ReLoop2-Backend-Health dashboard.
Part A — Set 7-Day Log Retention & Create Error Metric Filter Open CloudWatch -> Logs -> Log groups (ap-southeast-1) and select /aws/lambda/reloop2-api. Click Actions -> Edit retention setting(s) -> set 1 week (7 days) so workshop logs never accumulate storage indefinitely. Open /aws/lambda/reloop2-api -> Metric filters -> Create metric filter: Filter pattern: { $.msg = "unhandled_error" } Filter name: reloop2-UnhandledErrors Metric namespace: ReLoop/reloop2 Metric name: UnhandledErrors Metric value: 1, Default value: 0 Part B — Create SNS Alert Topic & Email Subscription Open Amazon SNS -> Topics -> Create topic: Type: Standard Name: reloop2-alarms Display name: ReLoop 2 Alarms Click Create subscription: Protocol: Email Endpoint: alerts@example.com (your real inbox; check your email and click Confirm subscription so SNS changes state from Pending confirmation to Confirmed!) Part C — Create 2 CloudWatch Alarms & Operational Dashboard Open CloudWatch -> Alarms -> Create alarm: Alarm 1 (reloop2-lambda-errors): Metric AWS/Lambda -> Errors (FunctionName = reloop2-api), Statistic Sum, Period 5 minutes, Condition >= 3 (1 of 1 datapoints), Treat missing data as Not breaching (notBreaching), Notify reloop2-alarms. Alarm 2 (reloop2-api-5xx): Metric AWS/ApiGateway -> 5xx (ApiId = <your HTTP API ID>), Statistic Sum, Period 5 minutes, Condition >= 5, Notify reloop2-alarms. Open CloudWatch -> Dashboards -> Create dashboard, name it ReLoop2-Backend-Health, and add 3 widgets: Lambda API (reloop2-api): Invocations, Errors, Throttles (Sum, 5 min line chart) HTTP API (<api-id>): Count, 4xx, 5xx (Sum, 5 min line chart) DynamoDB Capacity (reloop2-core-table): ConsumedReadCapacityUnits, ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits (Number sparkline)

title: Cleanup & Infrastructure as Code (Terraform)
content:
Because AWS WAFv2 charges continuously by the hour/month even with zero requests, always tear down all reloop2-* workshop resources in reverse dependency order once verification finishes. If you work alongside other environments, verify every name starts with reloop2 before confirming deletion.
Part A — Exact Reverse-Order Console Teardown Disable & Delete CloudFront Distribution (CloudFront -> Distributions, Global): select your distribution -> Disable -> wait until status transitions to Disabled -> Delete. Disabling first breaks dependencies on WAF reloop2-web, OAC, Functions, and reloop2-security-headers. Delete EventBridge Scheduled Rule (reloop2-sweep) (EventBridge -> Rules, ap-southeast-1): deleting the rule removes the scheduled target cleanly. Delete CloudWatch Alarms, Dashboard & SNS Topic (reloop2-*, ReLoop2-Backend-Health, ap-southeast-1): delete reloop2-lambda-errors, reloop2-api-5xx, Dashboard ReLoop2-Backend-Health, and SNS topic reloop2-alarms + its email subscription. Delete Regional WAF (reloop2-auth, ap-southeast-1): disassociate from reloop2-user-pool if still attached, then delete reloop2-auth. Delete HTTP API Gateway (reloop2-api, ap-southeast-1). Delete Bedrock Guardrail (reloop2-ai-guardrail). Delete Cognito Domain (reloop2-auth) & User Pool (reloop2-user-pool): first delete the domain prefix (Branding -> Domain), then click Delete user pool, check Deactivate deletion protection, and enter reloop2-user-pool. Delete CloudFront Edge WAF, OAC, Response Headers Policy & Functions (Global / us-east-1): once the CloudFront distribution finishes deleting: Delete Global WAF reloop2-web Delete Response Headers Policy reloop2-security-headers Delete Origin Access Control reloop2-web Delete CloudFront Functions reloop2-api-prefix and reloop2-spa-rewrite Empty & Delete Both S3 Buckets (reloop2-web-7k3q, reloop2-images-7k3q): because versioned or populated S3 buckets refuse direct deletion, select each bucket -> Empty -> type permanently delete, then click Delete -> enter the bucket name. Delete Lambda Functions (reloop2-api, reloop2-post-confirmation) & CloudWatch Log Groups (/aws/lambda/reloop2-*): note deleting a Lambda does NOT automatically remove its CloudWatch Log Group—delete both log groups explicitly! Delete DynamoDB Table (reloop2-core-table): keep Create an on-demand backup unchecked so you incur zero ongoing backup storage fees, type confirm, and delete. Delete IAM Roles (reloop2-api-lambda-role, reloop2-post-confirmation-role) & AWS Budget (reloop2-budget). Part B — Verify Zero Leftover Resources via AWS CLI After Console cleanup, verify across both regions that zero reloop2 resources remain:
aws s3api list-buckets --query "Buckets[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws dynamodb list-tables --region ap-southeast-1 --query "TableNames[?contains(@,'reloop2')]" aws lambda list-functions --region ap-southeast-1 --query "Functions[?contains(FunctionName,'reloop2')].FunctionName" aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --query "logGroups[?contains(logGroupName,'reloop2')].logGroupName" aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --region ap-southeast-1 --query "Items[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws cognito-idp list-user-pools --max-results 60 --region ap-southeast-1 --query "UserPools[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws wafv2 list-web-acls --scope CLOUDFRONT --region us-east-1 --query "WebACLs[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws wafv2 list-web-acls --scope REGIONAL --region ap-southeast-1 --query "WebACLs[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws cloudfront list-distributions --query "DistributionList.Items[?contains(Comment || '','reloop2')].Id" aws iam list-roles --query "Roles[?contains(RoleName,'reloop2')].RoleName" Part C — Reproducing Everything with Terraform (terraform/) Now that you understand every piece in the AWS Console, you can deploy or destroy the entire ReLoop stack in minutes using the modular Terraform (>= 1.6.0, hashicorp/aws >= 5.90) code included in this repository’s terraform/ directory:
File Managed Infrastructure provider.tf, data.tf, variables.tf Primary ap-southeast-1 + us_east_1 alias, CloudFront managed cache/origin policies, parameterized prefix & secrets storage.tf DynamoDB (PK/SK, GSI1, PITR, TTL), private images & web S3 buckets, CORS, 3 lifecycle rules, OAC bucket policy identity.tf Cognito User Pool, 4 groups, Managed Login v2 domain, PKCE client, post_confirmation IAM role + Python Lambda api.tf API Lambda IAM role + inline policy, Node.js 22 arm64 Lambda, HTTP API Gateway, JWT authorizer, 7 routes, throttling ai.tf Bedrock Guardrail (reloop2-ai-guardrail, APAC cross-region profile, Standard tier) + immutable Version 1 frontend.tf, functions/*.js OAC, CloudFront Functions (spa-rewrite.js, api-prefix.js), security-headers RHP, dual-origin CloudFront Distribution security.tf Edge WAF (reloop2-web, us-east-1) + Regional Cognito WAF (reloop2-auth, ap-southeast-1) + User Pool association events.tf, monitoring.tf, outputs.tf EventBridge 15m rule, Log retention + metric filter, SNS email topic, 2 Alarms, CloudWatch Dashboard, $5 AWS Budget Observed Engineering Notes from Live Import Verification This Terraform layout was imported and checked against the live reloop2 Console deployment (71 / 71 resources imported, 0 to destroy in terraform plan):
Breaking the CloudFront <-> CORS Dependency Cycle: CloudFront Distribution depends on the API Gateway domain and S3 website bucket, whereas Cognito callback URLs, S3 images CORS, and API Gateway CORS need the generated CloudFront domain. Keep cloudfront_cors_origins = [] on your initial terraform apply, read terraform output cloudfront_domain, then set cloudfront_cors_origins = ["https://<domain>"] and apply once more cleanly (just like Console Part 5.8 Part E). SNS Email Subscriptions (PendingConfirmation): AWS SNS does not return a subscription ARN until the recipient clicks the confirmation email link, so unconfirmed email subscriptions report PendingConfirmation until confirmed. Never Commit Secrets or State: Keep your real terraform.tfvars (containing origin_verify_secret and alert_email), terraform.tfstate*, .terraform/, and zip packages strictly out of Git using .gitignore — start by copying terraform.tfvars.example to terraform.tfvars. cd terraform cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # Populate alert_email, origin_verify_secret, and Lambda zip paths terraform init terraform plan terraform apply # After getting cloudfront_domain output, set cloudfront_cors_origins in terraform.tfvars and re-apply: terraform apply # Full cleanup when finished: terraform destroy
